nodes.title: Day 57 · What Is an Agent?
nodes.summary: Decide whether a problem genuinely needs an agent, and name the parts every agent needs.
checklist: The agent loop: Goal → decide what to do → act → look at the result → repeat until done.
Who decides what happens next: In a single call or a chain, your code decides the steps; in an agent, the model does.
Where agents help: Open-ended, multi-step tasks where you can't map out every step in advance.
When a chain is better: If you can write the steps down, a chain is simpler, cheaper and more reliable than an agent.
What an agent is made of: A model, instructions, tools, memory, a loop, and rules for when to stop.
Try it: List five tasks your users might want done. Mark which ones need an agent and which a simple chain could handle.
Outcome: Decide whether a problem genuinely needs an agent, and name the parts every agent needs.
Know: An agent is a model-driven loop (goal → act → observe → repeat) with stop rules; if you can write the steps, use a workflow.
Try: Sort five user jobs into workflow versus agent and write the stop condition for the agent-shaped ones.
Say in interview: I only use an agent when the path is unknown, and I can name the parts — model, tools, memory, limits.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 58 · The Agent Loop
nodes.summary: Explain how an agent loop works and build one that always stops.
checklist: Reason, then act (ReAct): The agent alternates between deciding what to do and doing it, using each result to choose the next step.
Build the loop yourself once: Using the tool calling you learned in Module 2, write a simple loop that keeps calling tools until the task is done.
When to stop: Set a maximum number of steps and a clear finish condition, and detect when the agent is repeating itself.
Step by step vs plan first: Some agents decide one step at a time; others write a plan first and then follow it.
Try it: Give your loop a task that needs three tool calls in a row. Then give it an impossible task and confirm your step limit stops it.
Outcome: Explain how an agent loop works and build one that always stops.
Know: ReAct-style loops fail by looping, skipping observation, or calling the wrong tool; the loop is only as good as the traces and caps.
Try: Run one task that should take two tools and log every thought, action and observation.
Say in interview: I can walk the loop on a whiteboard and I already know the failure modes I cap.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Days 59–60 · Building Agents with LangGraph
nodes.summary: Build a controllable agent in LangGraph and debug it by inspecting its state.
checklist: Why LangGraph: It gives you explicit control over each step, saves the agent's progress, and supports pausing for human approval.
State, nodes and edges: State holds what the agent knows; nodes do the work (call the model, run a tool, make a decision); edges decide what runs next.
Branches and loops: Use conditional edges to choose the next step and loops to repeat tool use until the task is done.
Ready-made vs custom: Start with LangGraph 's ready-made tool-using agent, then build your own graph when you need more control.
See what happened: Inspect the agent's state after a run to understand why it took the path it did.
Try it: Rebuild your Unit 5.2 loop as a LangGraph graph, then add a branch that sends simple questions straight to an answer without using tools.
Outcome: Build a controllable agent in LangGraph and debug it by inspecting its state.
Know: A graph framework (LangGraph or similar) is still your loop, state and edges; the library does not choose a good architecture for you.
Try: Draw the graph for one task (nodes, state keys, end conditions) before you write it, then implement that drawing.
Say in interview: I can show the state object and the edge that stops the run; I did not paste a template and hope.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 61 · Tools for Agents
nodes.summary: Give an agent a well-designed set of tools, including your own RAG system.
checklist: Your RAG pipeline becomes a tool: Wrap the RAG system from Module 4 as a search tool the agent can choose to use.
Tools the agent can choose between: Clear names, descriptions and inputs matter even more when the agent picks from several tools on its own.
Keep tool results small: Return only what the agent needs, so long results don't fill its context.
When tools fail: Return useful error messages so the agent can retry, try another tool, or give up gracefully.
Looking vs changing: Separate tools that only read information from tools that change things, and treat the second kind with care.

Try it: Give your agent your RAG search tool and a tool that takes an action, such as creating a support request. Ask one question that needs only search, and one task that needs search followed by an action.
Outcome: Give an agent a well-designed set of tools, including your own RAG system.
Know: A tool is a typed, least-privilege function with a description the model can follow; vague tools get misused.
Try: Rewrite one tool description after watching a bad call, and add a schema check that rejects extra arguments.
Say in interview: I design tools as APIs — name, schema, side effects, errors — and I change the description when traces show misuse.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 62 · Planning and Reflection
nodes.summary: Add planning and self-checking where they help, and leave them out where they don't.
checklist: Plan before acting: For longer tasks, have the agent write a short plan, then work through it.
Change the plan: Let the agent revise its plan when a step fails or new information appears.
Check its own work: Have the agent review its result before finishing and try again if it falls short.
The cost of thinking: More planning and checking can improve results but adds time and cost; use it where tasks are genuinely complex.
Try it: Give your agent a multi-part task with and without a planning step, and compare success, steps and cost.
Outcome: Add planning and self-checking where they help, and leave them out where they don't.
Know: Planning up front helps wide tasks; reflection after a step helps recovery; both cost tokens and can loop.
Try: Run one task with a written plan and one with a reflect-and-retry; keep the cheaper one that still succeeds.
Say in interview: I add planning or reflection only when a single ReAct pass fails, and I cap both.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 63 · Saving Progress and Asking for Approval
nodes.summary: Build an agent that saves its progress, resumes after interruptions, and waits for approval before acting.
checklist: Save as you go: LangGraph can save the agent's state after each step, so a long task survives a crash or restart.
Resume, don't restart: Pick up an interrupted run from where it stopped.
Pause for a human: Stop before important actions, show the person what the agent wants to do, and continue only once they approve.
Safe to retry: Design actions so that running them twice doesn't do the thing twice, such as creating the same support request again.
Try it: Add an approval step before a tool that changes something runs. Approve one request, reject another, and confirm the agent handles both.
Outcome: Build an agent that saves its progress, resumes after interruptions, and waits for approval before acting.
Know: Checkpointing lets you resume; an approval gate pauses before a risky tool and resumes with a human decision.
Try: Persist state after each step and insert one approval on a write tool; cancel once and resume once.
Say in interview: Risky actions wait for a person; progress is saved so a 'no' does not throw away the run.

links.title: Day 63 · Saving Progress and Asking for Approval (source)
Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 64 · MCP Fundamentals
nodes.summary: Explain how MCP works and connect your agent to existing MCP servers.
checklist: Why MCP exists: A standard way to connect AI apps to tools and data, so one integration works with many apps instead of being rebuilt for each.
Host, client and server: The app (host) uses a client to talk to MCP servers; each server exposes capabilities from one system.
What a server can offer: Tools the model can call, resources (data the app can read, such as files or records), and ready-made prompts.
Tool calling vs MCP: Tool calling is how a model asks for an action; MCP is how tools and data are packaged and shared between apps.
Using existing servers: Many systems already have MCP servers, such as file systems, code repositories and databases.
Connecting your agent: Use LangChain 's MCP support to load a server's tools into your LangGraph agent.
Try it: Connect your agent to an existing MCP server, such as a file-system server pointed at a folder of your documents, and ask it to find and summarize a file.
Outcome: Explain how MCP works and connect your agent to existing MCP servers.
Know: MCP is a standard way to expose tools and resources to any compatible client; it does not make those tools safe.
Try: Connect your agent to one existing MCP server and list the tools it advertised.
Say in interview: MCP is the plug; I still wrap auth, allow-lists and timeouts around whatever comes through it.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Days 65–66 · Building MCP Servers
nodes.summary: Package your own systems as MCP servers that any compatible app or agent can use.
checklist: Build your own server: Expose a real system, such as support requests, as an MCP server.
Tools, resources and prompts: Offer actions as tools (create or check a request), reference data as resources (your policies), and common tasks as prompts.
Good server design: Clear names and descriptions, typed inputs, useful error messages, and small, focused results, just like good tools in Module 2.
Local and remote servers: Servers can run on the same machine as the app or be reached over the internet; remote servers need authentication.
Test before you connect: Use an MCP inspector tool to call your server's tools directly and check what they return.
Several servers, one agent: Connect your agent to more than one server and make sure tool names don't clash or confuse it.
Changing a server safely: Adding or renaming tools changes what every connected agent sees; version your server and test agents after each change.

Try it: Build an MCP server for support requests with at least two tools and one resource. Test it with an inspector, connect your agent and an MCP-compatible AI app to it, and complete one task from each.
Outcome: Package your own systems as MCP servers that any compatible app or agent can use.
Know: An MCP server you publish is an API surface: versioned tools, clear errors, and no ambient credentials.
Try: Ship a tiny server with two tools and call it from a second process; break one tool and read the error.
Say in interview: I packaged a real system as MCP so other agents can use it, and I treated it like a public API.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Days 67–68 · Memory
nodes.summary: Build an agent that remembers what matters across conversations, keeps its memories accurate, and forgets on request.
checklist: Short-term and long-term: Short-term memory lasts for one conversation or task; long-term memory carries over between conversations.
Kinds of long-term memory: Facts about the user (preferences, details), records of past events (what happened last time), and lessons about how to do things better.
Where memories live: Store them in a database or LangGraph 's memory store, organized per user so they never mix.
When to save: During the conversation, when something important comes up, or in the background afterwards, so saving doesn't slow the user down.
What to save: Have the model pull out useful facts in a structured form, and avoid duplicates or saving every message.
When facts change: Update or replace memories that are out of date, and decide what wins when two memories disagree.
Recalling the right memories: Look up memories by relevance and recency, and add only the few that help with the current request.
Forgetting: Let memories expire, and delete them completely when a user asks, including from backups and logs.
Is memory helping?: Check whether the agent recalls the right things, and whether it ever remembers something wrong or outdated.

Try it: Tell your agent a preference ("always reply in Hindi") and a fact ("my team is in Pune") in one conversation. Check both are used in a new conversation, then change the fact and confirm the old one is replaced.
Outcome: Build an agent that remembers what matters across conversations, keeps its memories accurate, and forgets on request.
Know: Memory is what you persist, how you retrieve it, how you correct it, and how a user deletes it — not a vector store logo.
Try: Store two facts, retrieve them in a new session, then honor a 'forget this' request and prove they are gone.
Say in interview: Long-term memory is opt-in, inspectable and deletable; I never persist secrets or stale ACLs.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 69 · Context Engineering Basics
nodes.summary: Diagnose when an agent's problems are really context problems, and plan what goes into its context.
checklist: Context is a budget: Instructions, history, retrieved passages, memories, tool descriptions and tool results all compete for limited space.
Long runs go wrong: As context grows, agents lose track of the goal, miss details buried in the middle and cost more with every step.
See what's really in there: Inspect exactly what the agent sends the model at each step and spot what's useful and what's noise.
Split the budget: Give rough limits to each part: instructions, history, retrieved passages, memories and tool results.
Build it on purpose: Decide what's always included, what's looked up when needed, what's summarized and what's left out.
Order and label: Keep instructions, evidence, memories and user input clearly separated so the model doesn't mix them up.
Try it: Log the full context your agent sends at step 1, step 10 and step 20 of a long task. Measure how big each part has grown and mark what's no longer useful.
Outcome: Diagnose when an agent's problems are really context problems, and plan what goes into its context.
Know: Many 'the agent is dumb' bugs are context bugs: too much noise, the wrong tool result, or a lost goal.
Try: Print the exact tokens of one failing turn and cut or reorder them until the next action is correct.
Say in interview: I debug agents by reading the context I sent, not by switching the model first.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Days 70–71 · Compaction, Offloading and Tool Context
nodes.summary: Keep long, tool-heavy agent runs focused and affordable without losing the information that matters.
checklist: Summarize without losing the plot: Compress older history while keeping the goal, constraints, decisions and unfinished work.
Rolling summaries: Update a running summary as the task goes on instead of re-summarizing everything each time.
Keep exact details exact: Store numbers, IDs and other precise data separately, since summaries can blur them.
Write things down: Let the agent keep notes, plans and progress in a scratchpad or file outside its context and read them back when needed.
Trim tool results: Filter or summarize large results before they go back to the model, and keep the full version outside in case it's needed later.
Only the tools it needs: Load only the tools relevant to the current step, since every tool description takes space.
Use caching: Keep fixed instructions and tool descriptions at the start so they can be cached, and measure how much caching saves.
Give sub-tasks their own context: Hand a self-contained sub-task to a separate agent with a fresh context, so its working details don't crowd the main one; you'll build this in the multi-agent units.
Try it: Run a task of 20 or more steps three ways: keeping everything, summarizing history, and summarizing history plus trimming tool results and keeping notes. Compare success, tokens and cost.
Outcome: Keep long, tool-heavy agent runs focused and affordable without losing the information that matters.
Know: Compaction, offloading and slim tool results keep long runs inside the window and the budget.
Try: After a 10-step run, summarize old observations into a scratchpad and drop raw tool dumps; confirm the task still finishes.
Say in interview: I keep the goal, the last action and a compressed scratchpad; I do not resend every tool payload.

links.title: Days 70–71 · Compaction, Offloading and Tool Context (source)
Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 72 · Harness Engineering
nodes.summary: Improve an agent by changing its harness rather than its model, and prove each change with measurements.
checklist: What a harness is: Everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, instructions, tools, how context is built and trimmed, memory, permissions, approvals, error handling and the checks on its work.
The harness matters as much as the model: The same model can do very well or very badly depending on its harness; when an agent fails, the fix is usually in the harness, not a bigger model.
Designing the tool set: Choose between a few general tools and many narrow ones, decide what each tool's results show, and remove tools the agent rarely uses well.
Let the agent check its own work: Give it ways to verify results, such as running tests, validating output against a schema or re-checking a source, and feed errors back clearly so it can fix them.
Instructions on demand: Keep the core instructions short and load detailed guidance for a specific kind of task only when that task comes up.
Fit the harness to the model: Different models respond differently to the same tools and instructions; re-test your harness whenever you change models.
Change one thing at a time: Treat every harness change like a code change: make one change, run your test tasks, and keep it only if results improve.
Learn from existing harnesses: Study how well-known coding agents structure their loop, tools, instructions and checks.

Try it: Make three separate changes to your agent's harness: rewrite its tool descriptions, add a step that checks its answer against the retrieved sources, and load detailed instructions only for request-handling tasks. Measure each change on the same 10 tasks.
Outcome: Improve an agent by changing its harness rather than its model, and prove each change with measurements.
Know: The harness — tools, prompts, limits, memory, UI — is usually a bigger lever than swapping the model.
Try: Change one harness piece (tool schema or stop rule) and measure success rate and $ on the same 10 tasks.
Say in interview: I improve the harness and I prove it with a table; I do not start with a larger model.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 73 · Multi-Agent Patterns
nodes.summary: Choose a multi-agent pattern that fits the task, or decide that a single agent is better.
checklist: Why more than one agent: Different parts of a task may need different tools, instructions, models or permissions, and splitting work keeps each agent's context small.
Supervisor and specialists: One agent plans and hands work to specialist agents, then combines their results.
Handoffs: Agents pass a task along in sequence, each doing its part, like a support desk transferring a call.
Parallel specialists: Several agents work on parts of a task at the same time, and their results are merged.
Teams of teams: For large tasks, supervisors can manage other supervisors, each with their own specialists.
What goes wrong: Duplicated work, agents talking past each other, lost information between agents, conflicting results, and much higher cost.
One strong agent is often enough: Add more agents only when splitting the work clearly helps.
Try it: Sketch two designs for your agent: a single agent and a supervisor with specialists. For each, list which tools and permissions every agent gets, and predict which will cost more.
Outcome: Choose a multi-agent pattern that fits the task, or decide that a single agent is better.
Know: Multi-agent patterns (supervisor, handoff, parallel workers) add coordination cost; a single agent is the default.
Try: Pick one pattern for a two-skill task and write why a single agent would be worse — or admit it would not.
Say in interview: I choose a multi-agent shape from the task, or I keep one agent when the extra hops would only add spend.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Days 74–75 · Building Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.summary: Build a working multi-agent system and judge with numbers whether it beats a single agent.
checklist: Build a supervisor: Use LangGraph to build a supervisor that decides which specialist handles each part of a task.
Handoffs between agents: Pass a task, with the context it needs, from one agent to another.
What each agent sees: Decide whether agents share one state or pass messages, and give each only the information it needs.
Right tools, right model: Give each specialist only its own tools and permissions, and use cheaper models for simpler specialists.
Combining results: Merge specialists' outputs and resolve conflicts when they disagree.
When a specialist fails: Retry, reassign the work to another agent, or escalate to a person.
Track the cost: Measure steps, tokens, time and cost per agent and for the whole task.
Agents from other teams (A2A): A2A is an emerging standard for connecting agents built by different teams or companies, the way MCP connects tools.

Try it: Build a supervisor with two or three specialists, such as one for answering questions, one for handling requests and one for checking policies. Compare it with your single agent on the same ten tasks for success, cost and time.
Outcome: Build a working multi-agent system and judge with numbers whether it beats a single agent.
Know: A multi-agent demo without a single-agent baseline is not a result.
Try: Run the same 8 tasks on one agent and on your multi-agent graph; record success, steps and $.
Say in interview: Multi-agent beat single-agent on X and cost Y times more; I would ship the cheaper one if quality is tied.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 76 · Reliability and User Experience
nodes.summary: Build agents that fail predictably, hand over when stuck, and keep users informed and in control.
checklist: Common agent failures: Wrong tool, bad inputs, tools that are down, repeating itself, incomplete plans and running too long.
Budgets: Limit steps, time, retries and cost for every task.
Know when to hand over: When the agent can't continue safely, fall back to a simpler path or pass the task to a person.
Show progress: Let users see what the agent is doing, which tool it's using, and what it found.
Keep users in control: Let them cancel, pause, resume or change direction during long tasks.
Try it: Stream your agent's progress to the user step by step, and add a cost limit that stops any task above a set amount.
Outcome: Build agents that fail predictably, hand over when stuck, and keep users informed and in control.
Know: Users need to see progress, cancel, and take over; silent loops and surprise side effects are product bugs.
Try: Add a live step list and a cancel button to one run, and a handoff message when the agent is stuck.
Say in interview: The agent fails predictably, shows its work, and gives the user a way out.

nodes.title: Day 77 · Why Agent Evals Are Different
nodes.summary: Find your agent's most common failures by reading what it actually did, not just what it answered.
checklist: The final answer isn't enough: An agent can reach the right answer the wrong way, or the wrong answer for a fixable reason; you need to see the steps.
Read the traces: Look through 20 full agent runs step by step, using the tracing you set up in Module 2.
Group the failures: Note what went wrong in each run (wrong tool, bad inputs, loops, gave up early, lost context, bad handoff) and count each type.
What to measure: Decisions, tool use, the path taken, task success, recovery from problems, memory, efficiency and safety.
Try it: Read 20 traces from your agent, write a one-line note on each problem you find, and group them into failure types.
Outcome: Find your agent's most common failures by reading what it actually did, not just what it answered.
Know: Agent evals read trajectories — tool choice, order, recovery — not just the final paragraph.
Try: Score five traces as pass/fail on the path, not only the answer, and name the most common bad step.
Say in interview: I find failures by reading what the agent did; a pretty final report can still be a failed trajectory.

nodes.title: Day 78 · Evaluating Tool Use and Task Success
nodes.summary: Measure whether your agent makes good decisions and completes its tasks.
checklist: An agent test set: A list of tasks, each with what success looks like and, where it matters, the tools that should be used.
Right tool, right inputs: Check whether the agent picked the correct tool and filled in its inputs correctly.
A sensible path: Check for unnecessary tool calls, repeated steps, wrong order and stopping too early.
Did it get the job done?: Measure how often the agent completes each task successfully.
Judging the path: Use a model as a judge for whether the steps were reasonable, and check it against your own scores as you did in Module 4.
Try it: Build an agent test set of 15 tasks and score your agent on tool choice, inputs and task success.
Outcome: Measure whether your agent makes good decisions and completes its tasks.
Know: Tool-use accuracy and task success are different numbers; a lucky final answer can hide a dangerous call.
Try: Build a 10-task set with an explicit pass condition per task, including 'must not call X'.
Say in interview: I measure decisions and completion separately, and a forbidden tool call is an automatic fail.

nodes.title: Day 79 · Testing Recovery, Memory and Efficiency
nodes.summary: Measure how well your agent copes when things go wrong, whether its memory can be trusted, and what each task costs.
checklist: Break things on purpose: Make tools fail, return bad data or become unavailable, and leave out information the agent needs.
Did it notice and recover?: Check whether the agent retries, tries another tool, changes its plan or asks for help.
Test memory: Check that the agent recalls the right facts across conversations and never uses outdated or another user's memories.
Efficiency: Track steps, tool calls, tokens, time and cost per task alongside success.
Try it: Make your search tool fail on three tasks and return empty results on two more. Then run three tasks that depend on remembered facts. Record how the agent handles each.
Outcome: Measure how well your agent copes when things go wrong, whether its memory can be trusted, and what each task costs.
Know: Recovery after a tool error, memory correctness, and $ per task are as real as the happy-path success rate.
Try: Inject one tool failure and one stale memory; record whether the agent recovers and what it cost.
Say in interview: I test broken tools and bad memory on purpose, and I can quote cost per successful task.

nodes.title: Day 80 · Agent Threats and Least Privilege
nodes.summary: Explain how agents can be attacked and give yours only the access they truly need.
checklist: The dangerous combination: An agent that reads untrusted content, has access to private data or powerful tools, and has a way to send information out can be turned against its users.
Least privilege: Give each agent only the tools and permissions its task needs, and nothing more.
Check tool use in code: Validate which tool is used, its inputs and the user's permissions outside the model, before anything runs.
Memory can be attacked: Injected instructions saved as memories can affect every future conversation, and memories must never leak between users.
Limits stop runaways: Step, time and cost limits also protect against attacks designed to make the agent loop or spend.
Try it: List every tool and permission each of your agents has. For each one, write what an attacker could do with it, then remove or restrict anything not essential.
Outcome: Explain how agents can be attacked and give yours only the access they truly need.
Know: Agents expand the blast radius of injection because they can act; least privilege is the first control.
Try: List every tool permission and revoke one the task does not need; confirm the task still works.
Say in interview: Each tool has the narrowest credentials I can give it, because I assume a prompt can be hijacked.

nodes.title: Day 81 · Approval Gates and Sandboxing
nodes.summary: Let agents take powerful actions safely, with approval and isolation around anything risky.
checklist: Approval for anything irreversible: Sending messages, changing or deleting records, payments and running code should wait for a person.
Run generated code in a sandbox: Never run code the model writes inside your app; use an isolated environment such as E2B , Modal or a container.
Restrict the sandbox: Limit file access, network access, credentials, run time and computing power.
Generated commands are untrusted: Treat database queries, shell commands and web addresses written by the model as untrusted input.
Limit the damage: Design so that even a fully tricked agent can only do a small amount of harm.
Try it: Give your agent a tool that runs Python in a sandbox. Ask it to read a file outside the sandbox and to make a network request, and confirm both are blocked.
Outcome: Let agents take powerful actions safely, with approval and isolation around anything risky.
Know: Approval gates and sandboxes are how you let an agent touch email, money or a shell without hoping it is nice.
Try: Put one destructive tool behind approval and run it in a sandbox; take a screenshot of the wait state.
Say in interview: Powerful actions wait for a human and run isolated; I can show the gate in the trace.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 82 · Securing MCP and Tools
nodes.summary: Connect agents to MCP servers and tools without handing control to whoever wrote them.
checklist: Untrusted MCP servers: Connecting to someone else's MCP server gives them a way to influence your agent; treat third-party servers like third-party code.
Hidden instructions in tools: Tool descriptions and tool results can contain instructions aimed at the model, just like documents can.
Servers that change: A server you approved can change its tools or behavior later; review what it offers before every update.
Over-broad access: Give each server the narrowest permissions and credentials it needs.
Hijacked tool use: Injected instructions from documents or tool results may try to make the agent call tools it shouldn't; your code checks from Unit 5.19 are what stop them.
Try it: Change one tool description on your MCP server to include a hidden instruction, and one tool result to include another. See whether either changes your agent's behavior.
Outcome: Connect agents to MCP servers and tools without handing control to whoever wrote them.
Know: An MCP server is untrusted code from someone else's repo until you pin, wrap and allow-list it.
Try: Point your agent at a dummy MCP tool that asks for a secret and prove your wrapper strips it.
Say in interview: I pin MCP servers, wrap their tools, and I never forward ambient credentials.

links.title: Full roadmap · Level 5 for the deep version

nodes.title: Day 83 · Red-Teaming Your Agent
nodes.summary: Test your agent the way an attacker would and turn what you find into permanent tests.
checklist: Attack your own agent: Try to make it misuse tools, go beyond its permissions, reveal secrets, take actions without approval, poison its memory, or loop and run up costs.
Attack through every door: Use the user's messages, retrieved documents, tool results, MCP tool descriptions and saved memories.
Measure unsafe actions: Track how often attacks succeed and how often the agent attempts an action it shouldn't.
Every successful attack becomes a test: Add each attack that worked to your regression suite.
Safety vs usefulness: Check that your defenses haven't made the agent unable to do its job.
Try it: Write 10 attacks on your agent across messages, documents, tool results, MCP and memory. Record how many succeed, fix what you can, and run them again.
Outcome: Test your agent the way an attacker would and turn what you find into permanent tests.
Know: Red-teaming an agent means trying to make it act, not just say something naughty.
Try: Run five action-seeking attacks and turn each success into a CI case.
Say in interview: I test the way an attacker would — get a tool fired — and I keep those cases in the suite.

nodes.title: Day 84 · Designing an AI System
nodes.summary: Turn a product idea into a design you can defend, starting from requirements rather than favorite tools.
checklist: Start from the requirements: Who uses it, how many people, how fast it must respond, how good answers must be, what it may cost, and what data rules apply.
Rough numbers first: Turn expected users into requests per minute, tokens per day and cost per month before choosing anything.
Choose the simplest design that works: Decide between plain prompting, RAG , an agent or a mix, and justify each extra piece.
The core trade-offs: Quality, speed and cost pull against each other; every design choice favors one of them.
Plan for failure: Decide what happens when the model, a tool or a provider is down or slow.
Write it down: Record your design, the alternatives you rejected, and why.
Try it: Write a one-page design for your project: requirements, expected traffic, monthly cost estimate, a diagram of the main parts, and three decisions you made with the alternatives you rejected.
Outcome: Turn a product idea into a design you can defend, starting from requirements rather than favorite tools.
Know: A design starts from users, SLOs and constraints; frameworks come after the request path is clear.
Try: Write a one-page design for your project: questions, metrics, estimates, boxes, two deep dives, eval, rollout.
Say in interview: I start from requirements and a metric, not from the library I like, and I can defend the boxes.

nodes.title: Day 85 · From Prototype to Service
nodes.summary: Run your agent as a proper service that many users can use at once.
checklist: A backend for your agent: Put your agent behind a web API so any frontend or other app can use it.
Stream through the API: Send answers and agent progress to the user as they happen.
Know who's asking: Identify each user so permissions, memory and cost tracking work per person.
Keep the app stateless: Store conversations, agent progress and memories in a database, not inside the running app, so it can restart or scale without losing anything.
Long tasks in the background: Run long agent tasks as background jobs that report progress, instead of holding a request open.
Protect the API: Require authentication and limit how many requests each user can make.
Try it: Expose your agent through an API with a streaming endpoint. Call it from two different users and confirm each gets their own conversation and memories.
Outcome: Run your agent as a proper service that many users can use at once.
Know: A prototype script is not a service until it has an API, auth, concurrency limits and a process that can restart.
Try: Put your agent behind a small HTTP API and hit it with five overlapping requests.
Say in interview: Many users share one service; I can talk about queues, timeouts and what happens when a worker dies.

nodes.title: Day 86 · A Real Frontend
nodes.summary: Give users an interface that shows them what the agent knows, what it's doing and what it wants to do.
checklist: A chat interface: Build a simple chat page that streams answers as they arrive.
Show the evidence: Display citations so users can open the source of each claim.
Show what the agent is doing: Display progress, the tool in use and what it found during longer tasks.
Approval in the interface: Show the user exactly what the agent wants to do and let them approve or reject it.
Collect feedback: Add a simple way for users to rate answers and say what went wrong.
Handle failure in the interface: Show clear messages when something fails, and let users retry or cancel.
Try it: Build a chat page for your agent with streaming, citations, an approval prompt and a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on each answer.
Outcome: Give users an interface that shows them what the agent knows, what it's doing and what it wants to do.
Know: The UI should show retrieved context, live steps and pending approvals — not just a chat bubble.
Try: Add a panel that lists sources or tool calls while the answer streams.
Say in interview: Users see what the system knows and what it is about to do, so they can trust or stop it.

nodes.title: Days 87–88 · Packaging and Deploying
nodes.summary: Deploy your app reliably to a live environment, with secrets and settings kept safe and separate.
checklist: Package everything: Put your app in a container so it runs the same everywhere.
Run all the parts together: Package your app with its database and vector database so the whole system starts with one command.
Deploy to a managed host: Deploy to a hosting service that runs containers for you, so you don't manage servers yourself.
Secrets in the right place: Keep API keys and passwords in the host's secret storage, never in your code or container.
Separate environments: Keep development, testing and live versions apart, each with its own settings, data and keys.
Health checks: Let the host check that your app is running properly and restart it if not.
Data changes on deploy: Plan how database changes and re-indexing documents happen when you release a new version.
Try it: Deploy your app to a test environment, then to a live one. Change a setting only in the test environment and confirm the live one is unaffected.
Outcome: Deploy your app reliably to a live environment, with secrets and settings kept safe and separate.
Know: Deploy means an image, config and secrets that never live in the image, plus a rollback you have actually used.
Try: Dockerize, deploy once, rotate one secret, and write the rollback command.
Say in interview: I can ship and undo a release; secrets are env, and environments are separate.

nodes.title: Day 89 · Automatic Checks on Every Change
nodes.summary: Make it impossible to release a version of your app that's worse than the current one.
checklist: Test on every change: Run your tests automatically whenever you push code, using a tool such as GitHub Actions .
Your regression suite becomes a gate: Run your RAG quality, RAG security, agent and agent security tests, and block a release if any of them get worse.
Fast checks and full checks: Run a quick subset on every change and the full suite before each release, since evaluations cost time and money.
Prompts and models count as code: A changed prompt, model version or setting goes through the same checks as a code change.
Release only what passed: Build and deploy only the exact version that passed every check.
Try it: Set up automatic checks that run your quick test subset on every push. Push a deliberately worse prompt and confirm the release is blocked.
Outcome: Make it impossible to release a version of your app that's worse than the current one.
Know: CI that runs lint, tests and an eval threshold is how 'worse than prod' becomes unmergeable.
Try: Open a PR that drops the eval score and confirm the check fails.
Say in interview: A quality drop fails the build; that is the only way prompt changes stay honest.

links.title: Day 89 · Automatic Checks on Every Change (source)

nodes.title: Day 90 · Releasing Safely
nodes.summary: Release changes gradually, compare them on real traffic, and undo them quickly if they cause harm.
checklist: Every release can be traced: Record which code, prompt, model and settings are live, so any result can be traced to a version.
Release to a few users first: Send a small share of traffic to the new version and widen it only if it behaves well.
Test in the shadows: Run a new version on real questions without showing its answers to users, and compare it with the current one.
Compare versions with real users: Run two versions side by side and compare quality, user ratings and cost before choosing.
Turn features on and off: Release new behavior switched off and turn it on without a new deployment.
Roll back fast: Be able to return to the previous version in minutes when something goes wrong.
Try it: Release a new prompt to 10% of traffic, compare it with the current version on quality and cost, then either roll it out to everyone or roll it back.
Outcome: Release changes gradually, compare them on real traffic, and undo them quickly if they cause harm.
Know: Gradual rollout, a holdout, and a fast undo are how you release a model or prompt change.
Try: Write a release plan with a 5% canary, a kill switch, and the metric that trips it.
Say in interview: I canary on real traffic, compare to a holdout, and I can revert without a heroics story.

nodes.title: Days 91–92 · Watching It in Production
nodes.summary: Know how your app is performing for real users and turn what you see into improvements.
checklist: Trace live traffic: Keep tracing every request in production, so you can follow any user's problem step by step.
The numbers to watch: Requests, errors, response time (typical and slowest), tokens, and cost per request and per user.
Check quality on live traffic: Regularly score a sample of real answers with your judges, since live questions differ from your test set.
Listen to users: Collect ratings and comments, and watch signals like users rephrasing the same question or abandoning a task.
Spot changes over time: Notice when the questions people ask, your documents or the model's behavior start to shift.
Alerts: Get warned when errors, response times, costs or quality scores cross a limit you've set.
Close the loop: Add real failures and poorly rated answers to your test set, so the regression suite learns from production.
Keep private data out: Mask personal details in traces and logs, as you learned in Module 4.
Try it: Build a dashboard showing requests, errors, response time, cost and a live quality score. Set one alert, trigger it on purpose, and add three poorly rated answers to your test set.
Outcome: Know how your app is performing for real users and turn what you see into improvements.
Know: Production telemetry is quality samples, latency, $ and user outcomes — and a path from a bad trace back to the eval set.
Try: Pick one production-like failure and add it to your golden set the same day.
Say in interview: I watch real users and I turn what I see into eval cases; dashboards that nobody reads do not count.

nodes.title: Day 93 · Cost, Speed and Scale
nodes.summary: Make your app faster and cheaper without making it worse, and prove it with numbers.
checklist: Find where time and money go: Break each request into its parts (search, model calls, tools) and see which costs most.
Caching: Reuse answers to repeated questions, cache fixed prompt sections, and cache search results.
Answer similar questions once: Semantic caching reuses an answer when a new question means the same as an earlier one; decide which questions must never be answered from a cache.
Cheaper models for easy work: Send simple requests to a fast, cheap model and only hard ones to a stronger model.
Do things at the same time: Run independent steps in parallel instead of one after another.
Limits per user: Cap usage per user so one person or a runaway agent can't run up the bill.
Try it: Add caching and route simple questions to a cheaper model. Measure cost per request and response time before and after, and confirm your quality score hasn't dropped.
Outcome: Make your app faster and cheaper without making it worse, and prove it with numbers.
Know: Cost and latency come from tokens, retrieval, rerank and retries; you cut with numbers, not a new vendor logo.
Try: Take one slow or expensive request and apply one cut (cache, smaller model, shorter context); record quality.
Say in interview: I made it faster or cheaper without dropping the golden-set score, and I can show the before/after.

nodes.title: Day 94 · Model Gateways and Managed Platforms
nodes.summary: Avoid depending on a single provider, and know when a cloud AI platform is the right choice.
checklist: One gateway for all models: A model gateway sits between your app and model providers, holding keys, tracking usage and switching providers when one fails.
Backup providers: Fail over automatically when a provider is down or slow, knowing the backup model may answer differently.
Changing models is a release: A gateway can swap the model behind your app without a code change, so run your tests before every switch.
Cloud AI platforms: Many companies can't send data to a public API and use their cloud provider's AI platform instead, which serves models inside their own account.
Choosing a path: Compare public APIs, cloud AI platforms and hosting open models on data rules, cost, effort and how quickly you get new models.
Try it: Put a gateway in front of two model providers, make the main one fail, and confirm the backup answers within your response-time limit.
Outcome: Avoid depending on a single provider, and know when a cloud AI platform is the right choice.
Know: A gateway gives keys, budgets, routing and failover; a managed platform is a trade of control for ops load.
Try: List what you would put in a gateway versus leave in the product, and when you would just use a cloud AI API.
Say in interview: I avoid a single-provider hard dependency, and I can say when a platform is the right amount of control.

links.title: Day 94 · Model Gateways and Managed Platforms (source)

nodes.title: Day 95 · Serving Open Models Yourself
nodes.summary: Decide when serving an open model yourself is worth it, and choose the right way to host it.
checklist: Why host your own: Predictable cost at high volume, data that never leaves your control, and full control over which version runs.
The hosting ladder: Call an open model through a provider, rent GPUs from a platform that runs it for you, or run it on your own servers.
Serving software: Tools such as vLLM serve many requests efficiently by handling them together, which a simple loop can't do.
Smaller models, less memory: Compressed (quantized) versions of a model need far less memory, with some loss of quality.
Sizing the hardware: A model's size, its precision and the length of its inputs decide how much GPU memory you need.
Per token or per hour: Paying per token suits low or uneven traffic; renting GPUs by the hour wins only when they're kept busy.
Cold starts: A deployment that scales down to save money may answer its first request slowly.
Try it: Serve a small open model with vLLM or through a GPU platform. Send your test set through it and compare quality, response time and cost per thousand requests with your hosted model.
Outcome: Decide when serving an open model yourself is worth it, and choose the right way to host it.
Know: Self-hosting is worth it for privacy, cost at scale, or a custom model; it is a serving and paging problem, not a download.
Try: Write the memory math for one open model at your context and batch, and pick a serving stack on paper.
Say in interview: I can decide when to self-host, and I can talk prefill/decode and paging before I name a GPU.

nodes.title: Day 96 · Should You Fine-Tune?
nodes.summary: Decide whether a task justifies fine-tuning, and prepare a clean dataset and a fair baseline.
checklist: What fine-tuning changes: It teaches a model a behavior, format, style or narrow skill from examples; it's a poor way to add facts that change, which is what RAG is for.
Prompt, RAG or fine-tune: Try a better prompt first, add RAG for knowledge, and fine-tune only when your evals show those have run out.
When it wins: A consistent format or tone, a narrow task like classifying or extracting at high volume, specialist language, or replacing a large model with a small one to cut cost and response time.
What it costs: Collecting data, training, serving the tuned model, and tuning again whenever the base model changes.
Data is most of the work: Gather examples from your traces and test set, clean them, remove duplicates and personal data, and format them as conversations.
Quality beats quantity: A few hundred careful examples often beat thousands of messy ones.
Keep a held-out set: Set aside examples the model never trains on, and never train on your test set.
Examples from a stronger model: A stronger model can help write training examples; check the provider's terms first.

Try it: Pick a narrow task in your app, such as classifying incoming requests. Build 200 training examples from your traces and model-generated examples, plus 50 held-out examples, and measure how well your current prompted model does on the held-out set.
Outcome: Decide whether a task justifies fine-tuning, and prepare a clean dataset and a fair baseline.
Know: Fine-tune when behavior or cost needs a smaller specialist; do not fine-tune to add facts you could retrieve.
Try: Write a go/no-go with a baseline (prompt or RAG) and a clean train/held-out split.
Say in interview: I only fine-tune after a baseline loses on a measured set, and the data is clean enough to trust.

nodes.title: Day 97 · Fine-Tuning with LoRA
nodes.summary: Run a LoRA fine-tune, choose sensible settings, and spot when it's overfitting.
checklist: Full vs lightweight tuning: Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs a lot of hardware; LoRA trains a small add-on instead and gets most of the benefit.
Even less memory: QLoRA trains on a compressed model, so a small model can be tuned on a single modest GPU.
Choosing a base model: Pick a small open model that's good at your kind of task and whose license allows your use.
Tools: Libraries such as Hugging Face PEFT and Unsloth handle LoRA training; free notebook GPUs or rented GPUs are enough for small models.
Key settings: Learning rate, number of passes over the data and the size of the add-on; start from recommended values and change one thing at a time.
Watch for overfitting: If the model keeps improving on training data but gets worse on held-out data, stop.
Managed fine-tuning: Some providers tune models for you from an uploaded dataset, with no GPUs to manage; check where the tuned model lives and whether you can take it with you.
Forgetting other skills: Tuning hard on one task can make the model worse at others.
Try it: Fine-tune a small open model with LoRA on your 200 examples using a free notebook GPU, and record training and held-out results as it trains.
Outcome: Run a LoRA fine-tune, choose sensible settings, and spot when it's overfitting.
Know: LoRA trains a low-rank update; rank, steps and LR decide underfit versus memorization.
Try: Run one LoRA and plot train versus held-out; stop if held-out falls while train rises.
Say in interview: I can explain LoRA in a minute and I can spot overfitting on the held-out curve.

nodes.title: Day 98 · Evaluating, Serving and Distilling Fine-Tuned Models
nodes.summary: Prove with numbers whether a fine-tuned or distilled model earns its place, and serve it safely.
checklist: Beat the baseline or don't ship it: Compare the tuned model with your prompted model on the held-out set; keep it only if it's clearly better or much cheaper at the same quality.
Check what else changed: Run your full regression suite to catch anything the tune made worse.
Cost and speed: Compare cost and response time per request against the large model it might replace.
Learning from preferences: Preference tuning ( DPO ) teaches a model from pairs of better and worse answers, useful for tone and judgment.
Distillation: Use a strong model's answers to train a small model to do one task almost as well, much more cheaply.
Serving a tuned model: Merge the LoRA add-on into the model, or serve several add-ons on one base model with tools like vLLM .
Treat it like any release: Version the tuned model, release it gradually, and retrain when the base model or your data changes.

Try it: Compare your tuned small model with your prompted model on the held-out set for accuracy, cost and response time. Serve the tuned model, run your regression suite, and decide whether to use it.
Outcome: Prove with numbers whether a fine-tuned or distilled model earns its place, and serve it safely.
Know: A fine-tune or distill earns its place only if it beats the baseline on quality, $ and serving risk.
Try: Compare base vs LoRA vs a distilled student on the same 50 items and pick a winner in writing.
Say in interview: I serve the adapter (or the student) only when the table says it wins, and I keep a rollback to the base.

nodes.title: Day 99 · When Things Break
nodes.summary: Respond to production problems calmly and quickly, and make each one less likely to happen again.
checklist: Common incidents: A provider outage, sudden slowness, a cost spike, a drop in answer quality, or the agent looping.
Decide what to do: For each incident, know whether to roll back, switch provider, turn a feature off, or investigate first.
Runbooks: Write short step-by-step guides for your most likely incidents, so anyone can act quickly.
Find the cause: Use traces, dashboards and version records to work out what changed and when.
Learn from it: After each incident, write a short blameless review and add a test so it can't happen the same way again.
Try it: Write runbooks for two incidents: a provider outage and a sudden drop in answer quality. Then simulate one and follow your own runbook.
Outcome: Respond to production problems calmly and quickly, and make each one less likely to happen again.
Know: Incidents need a severity, a rollback, a comms line and a follow-up item in the eval or the runbook.
Try: Write a one-page incident for 'answers started citing the wrong tenant' and the first three actions.
Say in interview: I roll back first, then I add the case to the suite so the same break cannot silently return.

nodes.title: Day 100 · Whole-App Security Review
nodes.summary: Confirm that your complete, deployed app is secure from end to end, not just its individual parts.
checklist: Threat model the whole system: Map every path for untrusted input and every action that could cause harm, across the frontend, API, RAG system, agent, MCP servers, memory, models and logs.
Secrets and personal data everywhere: Check that no keys, passwords or personal details appear in code, containers, logs, traces, caches, test sets or fine-tuning data.
Checks at every boundary: Make sure user input, documents, tool results and model output are each checked where they enter or leave the system.
The API and frontend: Confirm authentication, per-user limits and permissions hold, and that answers can't send data to outside sites through links or images.
A final red-team: Attack the live app through every door, including the parts that only exist now that it's deployed.
Use the checklist: Run through the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications one last time against the finished app.
Try it: Run your full security test suite against the deployed app, then try five new attacks that target the API or frontend.

Know: A whole-app review walks auth, data, tools, logs, vendors and the UI — not just the prompt.
Try: Checklist your deployed app: keys, ACLs, tool perms, redaction, dependencies, and one leftover debug endpoint.

nodes.title: Project 5 · Voice Booking Agent (Advanced)
nodes.summary: A voice agent that books, changes and cancels appointments in a natural conversation, in English and mixed Hindi-English.
checklist: Keep the gap between the caller finishing and the agent replying short enough to feel natural, and measure it.
Handle interruptions, pauses and unclear speech.
Check availability and create bookings through tools, confirming details before saving.
Hand over to a person when the agent can't help.

nodes.title: Project 6 · Contract and Policy Comparer (Intermediate)

List additions, removals and changes, each linked to the exact text in both versions.
Flag changes in key areas such as payment, liability, termination and data use.
Never present the tool's output as legal advice.

Filter by price, category and other product details.
Compare joint image-text search with searching generated captions.
Measure search quality on queries with known correct results.

Ask for approval before submitting, paying or sending anything.
Recover when a page changes, loads slowly or shows an unexpected pop-up.
Resist instructions hidden in web pages that try to redirect the agent.

Build a clean training set and a held-out test set that the model never trains on.
Measure a prompted large model as the baseline.
Fine-tune with LoRA, then compare accuracy, cost and response time.
Serve the tuned model behind an API.
