nodes.title: Interview Q1–12 · LLM Fundamentals
nodes.summary: 12 interview questions on llm fundamentals. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q1 (Concept): What does an LLM actually do when it generates text? A strong answer covers: It predicts the likelihood of every possible next token, picks one, adds it, and repeats; it's not looking up stored answers; sampling settings decide how the next token is picked; this explains both its flexibility and its fluent mistakes.

Q2 (Concept): What is a token, and why do token counts matter? A strong answer covers: Tokens are pieces of words that models read and charge by; they set cost, how much fits in the context window and how long generation takes; Hindi, mixed-language text, code and numbers often use more tokens for the same meaning.

Q3 (Concept): Why do LLMs make things up? A strong answer covers: Models are trained to produce plausible text, not to check facts; gaps in knowledge, vague questions and missing context make it worse; reduce it with retrieval, citations, permission to say "I don't know", output checks and evals that measure it.

Q4 (Concept): What is the context window, and why isn't a bigger one always better? A strong answer covers: Instructions, history, documents, tool results and the answer all share one limit; long inputs cost more and respond slower; models often miss details buried in the middle; choosing the right context beats sending more.

Q5 (Concept): How does temperature affect output, and how do you choose it? A strong answer covers: Low temperature makes output more predictable, high makes it more varied; use low for extraction, classification and facts, higher for brainstorming; reasoning models may ignore it; check consistency by running the same input several times.

Q6 (Concept): Why does a long answer take longer than a long question? A strong answer covers: The input is processed largely in parallel, but the answer is generated one token at a time; time to first token and tokens per second are separate measures; streaming improves how fast it feels; capping output length cuts both time and cost.

Q7 (Scenario): When would you use a reasoning model, and when wouldn't you? A strong answer covers: Reasoning models help on multi-step logic, math, code and planning; they waste money and time on extraction, rewriting and simple classification; decide by testing both on your own examples and comparing accuracy, cost and speed.

Q8 (Concept): What's the difference between a base model and a chat model? A strong answer covers: A base model is trained only to continue text; chat models get extra training on instructions and human feedback; that's why they follow instructions, answer conversationally and refuse some requests.

Q9 (Scenario): How would you choose a model for a new feature? A strong answer covers: Define the task and its requirements (quality, speed, cost, context size, data rules, features like tool calling); shortlist using public rankings; test on your own examples; look at the failures, not just the score; pin the version you choose.

Q10 (Concept): Why can't you trust leaderboard rankings for your use case? A strong answer covers: Leaderboards use other people's tasks, prompts and definitions of a good answer; test questions may have leaked into training data; old benchmarks are saturated; use rankings to shortlist, then decide on your own data.

Q11 (Concept): How do API models and open-weight models compare? A strong answer covers: API models offer top capability and no infrastructure but less control and data leaves your boundary; open models offer control, privacy and cheaper costs at high volume but need hosting work; check licenses; hosted open models are a middle path.

Q12 (Concept): How do models handle images and PDFs, and what goes wrong? A strong answer covers: Images become tokens and cost more at higher resolution; digital PDFs have text, scanned ones are images; models struggle with counting, tiny text, exact table values and invent details; send clean text when you have it.

nodes.title: Interview Q13–22 · Building with LLM APIs
nodes.summary: 10 interview questions on building with llm apis. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q13 (Concept): LLM APIs don't remember anything. How do you build a multi-turn chat? A strong answer covers: Your app stores the conversation and sends the history with every request; history grows cost and length, so trim or summarize it; what your app stores and what you send the model are separate decisions.

Q14 (Concept): How does tool calling work from start to finish? A strong answer covers: You describe tools to the model; it returns a tool name and inputs instead of an answer; your code checks the inputs and runs the tool; you send the result back with its ID; the model continues or answers; it may call several tools.

Q15 (Concept): How do you get structured output you can rely on? A strong answer covers: Use the model's structured-output feature with a schema, not "please return JSON"; validate every result; retry, repair or reject failures; remember that valid format doesn't mean correct content.

Q16 (Concept): What makes a good tool for an LLM? A strong answer covers: A precise name and description of when to use it, few typed inputs, small and useful results, clear error messages, and no overlap with other tools; the description is effectively part of the prompt.

Q17 (Scenario): Which API errors should you retry, and how? A strong answer covers: Retry temporary failures such as rate limits, server errors and timeouts, with growing waits, a little randomness and a cap on attempts; fail fast on bad keys and invalid requests; set timeouts on every call; fall back to another model when needed.

Q18 (Concept): What is streaming, and why use it? A strong answer covers: The answer is sent piece by piece as it's generated; it cuts the time until users see something without making the total faster; you still assemble and save the full response; handle cancellations and broken streams.

Q19 (Scenario): When would you use a framework like LangChain instead of calling the API directly? A strong answer covers: Frameworks speed up common patterns, switching providers and integrations; they add abstraction that can make debugging harder; either way you need to understand the underlying calls; choose based on the project, not popularity.

Q20 (Scenario): How would you run 10,000 documents through an LLM efficiently? A strong answer covers: Estimate cost first; run requests concurrently with a limit to respect rate limits; use cheaper batch APIs when results aren't urgent; retry failed items individually; save results as you go so a crash doesn't restart everything.

Q21 (Concept): What should you record for every LLM request? A strong answer covers: Model and version, prompt version, input and output tokens, time taken, cost, retries, errors and tool calls; link the steps of one user request into a single trace; keep personal data out of logs.

Q22 (Concept): What's the difference between a chain and an agent? A strong answer covers: In a chain your code decides the steps; in an agent the model decides; chains are cheaper, faster and more predictable; use an agent only when the steps genuinely can't be known in advance.

nodes.title: Interview Q23–30 · Prompt Engineering
nodes.summary: 8 interview questions on prompt engineering. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q23 (Concept): What goes into a good system prompt? A strong answer covers: The app's purpose, how it should behave, what it must not do, what to do when information is missing or out of scope, and what a good answer looks like; a few clear rules beat a long rulebook; keep per-request details out of it.

Q24 (Concept): When do few-shot examples help, and how do you choose them? A strong answer covers: Use them when the format or judgment you want is hard to describe; pick varied examples, including a tricky case; models copy examples closely, and order can matter; they add tokens to every request.

Q25 (Scenario): How do you know a prompt change is actually an improvement? A strong answer covers: Score both versions on the same test set, never on one good answer; run each more than once to check consistency; compare cost and speed too; keep some questions aside to confirm the gain.

Q26 (Concept): How do you prompt a reasoning model differently? A strong answer covers: Skip "think step by step"; give the goal, the relevant context, the constraints and what a good answer looks like; avoid micro-managing its steps; measure whether the extra reasoning pays for itself.

Q27 (Concept): What is prompt caching, and how do you design for it? A strong answer covers: Providers charge less for a prompt start they've recently seen; put fixed instructions and documents first and changing parts last; measure how often the cache is used and what it saves.

Q28 (Concept): What is prompt injection, and why can't a prompt alone stop it? A strong answer covers: Text from users or documents that tries to override your instructions, typed directly or hidden in content; models can't reliably tell instructions from data; real protection is in code: limited permissions, checked tool calls, output checks and human approval.

Q29 (Scenario): How do you manage prompts in production? A strong answer covers: Version prompts like code and record which version and model produced each result; test changes against the regression suite before release; roll out gradually; be able to roll back.

Q30 (Concept): Can you use a model to improve your prompts? A strong answer covers: Yes, by giving a model your prompt and its failures, or with tools like DSPy that search for better instructions and examples; score every candidate on a test set; judge the winner on held-out questions to avoid overfitting; read what it produced.

nodes.title: Interview Q31–50 · RAG
nodes.summary: 20 interview questions on rag. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q31 (Scenario): When should you use RAG, and when shouldn't you? A strong answer covers: Use it for private, changing or large knowledge and when answers need sources; skip it when the model already knows enough, the task is just transforming text, or everything fits in the prompt; fine-tuning is for behavior, not facts.

Q32 (Concept): Walk me through a RAG pipeline. A strong answer covers: Load and clean documents, split them into passages, embed and store them with their details; at question time, search, optionally rerank, assemble the best passages into the prompt, and generate an answer with citations.

Q33 (Scenario): How do you choose a chunking strategy? A strong answer covers: Follow the document's own structure where possible; small passages are precise but lose context, large ones keep context but add noise; keep titles and sections with each passage; compare options on a retrieval test set.

Q34 (Concept): What are embeddings, and how do you choose an embedding model? A strong answer covers: Lists of numbers that place similar meanings close together; choose on retrieval quality with your own data and languages, plus cost and speed; embeddings from different models can't be mixed, so changing models means re-embedding.

Q35 (Concept): Why use hybrid search? A strong answer covers: Meaning-based search misses exact names, codes and numbers; keyword search catches them; combining both, for example with reciprocal rank fusion, works best on technical or mixed questions; measure the gain.

Q36 (Concept): What does a reranker do, and when is it worth it? A strong answer covers: It reads the question and each candidate passage together to judge relevance more accurately; retrieve many, rerank, keep the best few; it adds time and cost; measure whether it improves answers for your data.

Q37 (Scenario): A user's question is vague or has several parts. How can retrieval still work? A strong answer covers: Rewrite it into a clearer query, search with several versions and combine results, search with a draft answer, or split it into sub-questions; each adds calls, so use them only where they help.

Q38 (Scenario): How do you handle tables, scans and messy PDFs? A strong answer covers: Use layout-aware parsers, text recognition or vision models for scans; keep tables whole with their headers; check extracted text against the original on samples; use the expensive approach only for documents that need it.

Q39 (Scenario): How would you answer questions that need numbers from a database? A strong answer covers: Text-to-SQL with the table structure and column descriptions; read-only access, query checks and row limits; retry failed queries within a limit; show the query or figures; route each question to documents, the database or both.

Q40 (Concept): What is self-correcting RAG? A strong answer covers: Grade the retrieved passages and search again or fall back if they're weak; check the answer is supported before returning it; search in steps for multi-part questions; always cap retries to control cost.

Q41 (Scenario): When is Graph RAG worth the effort? A strong answer covers: For questions about relationships or about a whole collection that no single passage answers; it's expensive to build and keep up to date; add it only when measured failures show plain retrieval can't cope.

Q42 (Scenario): How do you stop a RAG system from making things up? A strong answer covers: Instruct it to answer only from the passages; require citations and check they support the claims; let it say "I don't know" when evidence is weak; improve retrieval; measure faithfulness on a test set.

Q43 (Concept): How do you evaluate a RAG system? A strong answer covers: Test retrieval on its own (did it find the right passage) and generation on its own (is the answer supported and relevant), then the full pipeline and user-facing quality; track cost and speed alongside.

Q44 (Scenario): How do you build a good test set for a RAG app? A strong answer covers: Real questions with expected answers and source passages; include unanswerable, ambiguous and multi-part questions; use a model to suggest more but check each one yourself; keep adding real failures from production.

Q45 (Concept): How do you know your model-as-a-judge can be trusted? A strong answer covers: Score a sample yourself and measure agreement; ask one clear pass-or-fail question per check; watch for biases toward longer answers, the first option or its own outputs; fix the judge until it agrees with you.

Q46 (Debugging): Retrieval finds the right passages, but answers are still wrong. What do you check? A strong answer covers: How passages are assembled (too many, bad order, conflicting documents), the prompt, and whether the model answers faithfully when given the correct passages directly; test each piece separately to find the cause.

Q47 (Scenario): How do you make sure changes don't make your app worse? A strong answer covers: A versioned test set and a baseline; run the evaluation automatically on every change to prompts, settings, models or code; block releases that score worse; watch quality, cost and speed together.

Q48 (Concept): What is indirect prompt injection in a RAG app, and how do you defend against it? A strong answer covers: Hidden instructions inside retrieved documents; treat retrieved text as data, never commands; limit what the model can do and check tool calls in code; check outputs for data-leaking links; control who can add documents.

Q49 (Scenario): How do you make sure users only see documents they're allowed to see? A strong answer covers: Store permissions with each passage and filter during search, not after the answer; keep customers fully separated; check caches, memory and citations, which can also leak restricted information.

Q50 (Scenario): How do you handle personal data in a RAG system? A strong answer covers: Detect and remove or mask it before indexing; keep it out of logs, traces and test sets; delete it everywhere when required; know your model provider's data retention; know the data protection rules that apply, such as India's DPDP Act.

nodes.title: Interview Q51–70 · Agents
nodes.summary: 20 interview questions on agents. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q51 (Concept): What is an AI agent, and when should you not build one? A strong answer covers: A model that decides its own next step in a loop, using tools until a goal is met; worth it for open-ended, multi-step tasks; when the steps can be written down, a fixed workflow is cheaper and more reliable.

Q52 (Concept): Explain the ReAct pattern. A strong answer covers: The model alternates between deciding what to do and doing it, looks at each result, and decides again; it needs clear tools and stopping rules; planning first is an alternative for longer tasks.

Q53 (Scenario): How do you stop an agent from looping forever or overspending? A strong answer covers: Limits on steps, time, retries and cost; detecting repeated actions; clear finish conditions; handing over to a person when stuck; budgets checked in code, not left to the model.

Q54 (Concept): Why use a framework like LangGraph for agents? A strong answer covers: Explicit state, steps and branches you can inspect; saving progress so runs can resume; pausing for human approval; easier debugging than a hand-written loop as agents grow.

Q55 (Scenario): How do you add human approval to an agent? A strong answer covers: Pause before any action that changes something; show exactly what the agent wants to do; let the person approve, reject or edit; resume from saved state; make actions safe to retry.

Q56 (Concept): What is MCP, and how is it different from tool calling? A strong answer covers: Tool calling is how a model asks for an action; MCP is a standard for packaging tools, data and prompts in servers that any compatible app can connect to; host, client and server roles.

Q57 (Design): How would you design an MCP server for an internal system? A strong answer covers: A few focused tools with clear descriptions and typed inputs, resources for reference data, useful errors and small results, authentication, minimal permissions, versioning, and testing with more than one app.

Q58 (Concept): How do you give an agent memory? A strong answer covers: Short-term memory within a task and long-term memory across conversations; store useful facts, past events and lessons rather than every message; look up only relevant memories; update, expire and delete them; keep each user's memories separate.

Q59 (Concept): What is context engineering, and why does it matter for agents? A strong answer covers: Deciding what goes into the model's context at each step; context fills up fast in long runs and quality drops; summarize history, trim tool results, keep notes outside the context, load only needed tools, and cache fixed parts.

Q60 (Scenario): How do you keep a long-running agent on track? A strong answer covers: Summaries that keep the goal, decisions and unfinished work; plans and notes stored outside the context; trimmed tool results; sub-agents with fresh context for side tasks; saved progress so it can resume.

Q61 (Concept): What is harness engineering? A strong answer covers: Everything around the model that makes it an agent: the loop, instructions, tools, context handling, checks on its work and permissions; most agent failures are fixed in the harness, not by a bigger model; change one thing at a time and measure.

Q62 (Scenario): When is a multi-agent system better than a single agent? A strong answer covers: When parts of the task need different tools, permissions or models, or benefit from separate context and parallel work; costs include coordination, lost information between agents and higher spend; prove it beats one agent with numbers.

Q63 (Concept): Describe common multi-agent patterns. A strong answer covers: A supervisor that delegates to specialists, handoffs in sequence, parallel specialists whose results are merged, and teams of teams; match the pattern to how the work naturally divides.

Q64 (Concept): How do you evaluate an agent? A strong answer covers: Task success, choosing the right tools with the right inputs, a sensible path without loops or wasted steps, recovery from failures, cost and time per task, and safety; read traces; check any judge against your own scores.

Q65 (Scenario): How do you test whether an agent copes when things go wrong? A strong answer covers: Make tools fail, return bad data or go missing on purpose; check whether it retries, switches approach or hands over; measure recovery rate, not just success when everything works; add these cases to the regression suite.

Q66 (Concept): Why are agents riskier than chatbots? A strong answer covers: Agents take actions with real effects; the dangerous mix is untrusted input, access to private data or powerful tools, and a way to send data out; defend with minimal permissions, checks in code, approval and sandboxing.

Q67 (Scenario): How do you let an agent run code safely? A strong answer covers: Run it in an isolated sandbox, never in your app; restrict file access, network, credentials, time and resources; treat any code, queries or commands the model writes as untrusted; return only the needed output.

Q68 (Concept): What are the security risks of connecting to third-party MCP servers? A strong answer covers: Hidden instructions in tool descriptions or results, servers changing behavior after you approved them, and over-broad permissions; review servers like third-party code, pin versions and give each the narrowest access.

Q69 (Scenario): How do you red-team an agent? A strong answer covers: Attack through user messages, documents, tool results, MCP and memory; try to make it misuse tools, exceed permissions, leak secrets or act without approval; measure how often attacks succeed; fix and add each one to the regression suite.

Q70 (Debugging): An agent works in testing but fails in production. How do you debug it? A strong answer covers: Read production traces; compare real inputs with your test cases; check tool errors and slowness, context growth, and recent model or prompt changes; reproduce the failure; add it to the test set.

nodes.title: Interview Q71–85 · Shipping to Production
nodes.summary: 15 interview questions on shipping to production. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q71 (Scenario): How would you take an LLM app to production? A strong answer covers: An API with streaming, state kept in a database so the app can restart or scale, containers, a managed host, secrets kept out of code, separate test and live environments, health checks, authentication and per-user limits.

Q72 (Scenario): How do you stop a prompt change from breaking production? A strong answer covers: Treat prompts as code, run the regression suite automatically and block worse versions, release to a small share of users first or test in the shadows, and roll back fast if needed.

Q73 (Concept): What would you monitor for an LLM app? A strong answer covers: Requests, errors, typical and slowest response times, tokens, cost per request and per user, a live quality score on sampled answers, user feedback, and shifts in what users ask; alerts on each.

Q74 (Scenario): How do you collect and use user feedback? A strong answer covers: Explicit ratings and comments plus signals like rephrasing or giving up; review them regularly; turn real failures into test cases; remember that feedback is sparse and biased toward unhappy users.

Q75 (Scenario): How would you cut your LLM costs in half? A strong answer covers: First measure where cost goes; then cache repeated answers and prompt prefixes, send simple requests to cheaper models, shorten prompts and outputs, use batch APIs, or fine-tune a small model; confirm quality didn't drop.

Q76 (Scenario): How do you make an LLM app faster? A strong answer covers: Stream answers, use smaller or faster models where possible, run independent steps in parallel, remove unnecessary sequential calls, cache, shorten outputs, and measure which step is actually slow first.

Q77 (Concept): What is semantic caching, and what are the risks? A strong answer covers: Reusing an answer when a new question means the same as an earlier one; a wrong match returns a wrong answer; cached answers go stale; never share cached answers across users with different permissions or personal data.

Q78 (Concept): What is a model gateway, and why use one? A strong answer covers: One endpoint in front of several providers that handles keys, budgets, routing, failover and usage tracking; it becomes a critical dependency itself; providers aren't interchangeable, so test before switching.

Q79 (Scenario): When would you host an open model yourself? A strong answer covers: Strict data rules, high and steady volume, or the need for full control; costs include GPUs, operations and possibly lower quality; compare per-token and per-hour pricing at your real volume; use efficient serving and compressed models.

Q80 (Scenario): When should you fine-tune instead of using prompting or RAG? A strong answer covers: Fine-tune for behavior, format, style or a narrow high-volume task, or to replace a large model with a small one; not for adding facts that change; only after better prompts and RAG have measurably run out.

Q81 (Concept): Explain LoRA and why it's popular. A strong answer covers: It freezes the base model and trains a small add-on, so it needs far less memory and compute; QLoRA goes further by training on a compressed model; add-ons are small and can be swapped on one base model.

Q82 (Scenario): How do you know a fine-tune actually worked? A strong answer covers: Compare it with a prompted baseline on a held-out set it never trained on; run the full regression suite to catch skills it lost; compare cost and speed; check that test data didn't leak into training.

Q83 (Concept): What is distillation? A strong answer covers: Training a small model on a larger model's outputs for a specific task, so it performs almost as well for much less; check the provider's terms; evaluate it like any other model.

Q84 (Scenario): Your main model provider has an outage. What happens in your app? A strong answer covers: Automatic failover to a backup provider through a gateway, graceful degradation, cached answers where safe, clear messages to users, alerts and a runbook; failover should be tested before it's needed.

Q85 (Scenario): How do you roll out a new model version safely? A strong answer covers: Pin versions so nothing changes silently; run the full evaluation suite; try it on real traffic in the shadows or on a small share of users; watch quality, cost and speed; keep a rollback ready.

nodes.title: Interview Q86–91 · System Design
nodes.summary: 6 interview questions on system design. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q86 (Design): Design a customer support assistant for a company with 10,000 help articles and 50,000 users a day. A strong answer covers: Traffic and cost estimates; RAG with hybrid search and reranking; citations and handing over to a human; caching common questions; routing simple questions to cheaper models; evals, monitoring and feedback; fallback providers.

Q87 (Design): Design an assistant over a company's internal documents with strict access control. A strong answer covers: Permissions applied during search, separation between teams, deployment inside the company's cloud or a private platform, audit logs, personal-data handling, and tests proving users can't see restricted content.

Q88 (Design): Design a system that extracts data from one million scanned invoices a month. A strong answer covers: A batch pipeline with parsing and vision models, schema validation, confidence scores and human review, throughput and cost per document, cheaper models for easy documents, and accuracy monitoring.

Q89 (Design): Design a coding assistant that can fix bugs in a large codebase. A strong answer covers: Searching and selecting relevant code, managing context, running tests in a sandbox, proposing changes for human approval, measuring success on real past issues, and controlling cost per task.

Q90 (Design): Design a voice agent that books appointments. A strong answer covers: Speech-to-text, model and text-to-speech in sequence versus a single speech model; a tight response-time budget; detecting when the caller has finished; handling interruptions; booking tools with confirmation; handing over to a person.

Q91 (Design): Design a research agent that produces cited reports. A strong answer covers: Planning sub-questions, parallel search agents with separate context, checking every citation, time and cost budgets, long-running jobs with progress updates, and evaluating report accuracy.

nodes.title: Interview Q92–96 · Debugging Scenarios
nodes.summary: 5 interview questions on debugging scenarios. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q92 (Debugging): RAG quality was fine at launch but dropped after a few weeks. How do you investigate? A strong answer covers: Find what changed (documents, index, model version, prompt, the kinds of questions users ask); run the test set on the current version; test retrieval and generation separately; check for stale or duplicated documents; add the failures as tests.

Q93 (Debugging): Your agent suddenly costs three times more per task. What do you check? A strong answer covers: Traces for more steps, loops or retries; growing context or larger tool results; a routing or model change; a drop in cache hits; then add or tighten cost and step limits.

Q94 (Debugging): Response times doubled overnight. What do you do? A strong answer covers: Find which step is slow (provider, search, tools, your own code); check traffic, rate limits and output length; fail over or degrade if it's the provider; follow the runbook and alert the right people.

Q95 (Scenario): A prompt change improves quality but doubles cost. Do you ship it? A strong answer covers: Put a value on the quality gain against the extra cost; find where the extra tokens come from; try to keep the gain more cheaply (caching, a cheaper model for part of the work); if you ship, roll out gradually and watch both.

Q96 (Debugging): Users say the assistant is making things up. How do you respond? A strong answer covers: Collect real examples; sort them into retrieval misses, unsupported answers and outdated documents; measure faithfulness; strengthen "I don't know" behavior and citations; fix the root cause and add the cases to the test set.

nodes.title: Interview Q97–100 · Your Projects
nodes.summary: 4 interview questions on your projects. Tick a question once you can answer it out loud and your answer covers each point listed.
checklist: Q97 (Defense): Walk me through a project you built. A strong answer covers: The problem and who it's for, the simple baseline, the design and key decisions with the alternatives you rejected, results with numbers, a failure and what you changed, and what you'd do next.

Q98 (Defense): Why did you use RAG, an agent or fine-tuning instead of something simpler? A strong answer covers: What you tried first, the measured shortcoming that justified the extra complexity, and the cost of that complexity; if you can't show the numbers, say what you'd measure.

Q99 (Defense): What would break first if your project had 100 times the traffic? A strong answer covers: Rough capacity numbers; the likely first bottleneck (rate limits, database, search, cost); and how you'd fix it with caching, scaling, cheaper models or queues.

Q100 (Defense): How do you keep up with AI without chasing hype? A strong answer covers: A repeatable process: follow primary sources, test new models and tools on your own test set, compare cost and speed, and roll out gradually; give a real example of something you adopted or rejected and why.
